source_read: PDF, Lancet 9 June 1973, pp. 1267–1271, all five scanned pages read on renders at 110 dpi, with Tables I to III and the Growth paragraph re-read at 250 dpi; every number used was checked on the image (the text layer lacks the three tables); p. 1271 also carries the start of an unrelated article

claims.overstatement: None. The claim calls the report a description of eight selected children, attributes both the 'first' and the causal conclusion to the authors, and lists the design's limits; no drinking amounts appear.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude was checked on the rendered pages; the derivable means were recomputed and reproduce (anchor on Table I). Table II totals agree with the per-child marks and the case reports. Small points, none changing the verdict: (1) ascertainment — besides the four first children and the two found by their features, the last two were found because their mothers had alcoholism (p. 1267); the claim names only the first six. (2) Patient 5's information came from Akron Children's Hospital and he was examined by D.W.S. (p. 1271) and tested on a different scale, not by A.P.S. (pp. 1269–1270), so 'evaluated at a dysmorphology unit in Seattle' holds for seven of the eight; the methods' statement that all eight were examined together by the same two observers is not fully consistent with this. (3) The paper does say drinking was excessive throughout the pregnancy, so 'timing ... not recorded' should read 'timing not measured beyond that statement'. (4) On nutrition, Table I shows weight loss during the pregnancy in four of the six mothers with data (1, 5, 15 and 5 lb) and gain in two (19 and 30 lb), which bears on the undernutrition explanation the authors argue against; worth adding to 'nutrition was only partly recorded'. (5) The 26.6 g and 24.4 g comparison figures are from a personal communication, and the number of children behind the 65% and 38% averages is not stated. (6) The 'first' is the authors' own judgement; their Introduction credits a co-author's 1972 paper with having already noted growth deficiency and developmental delay in such children. The source confirms the date (9 June 1973), which fits the claim's point that the reviews date the first description to November 1973.

anchors.extracted: The eight unrelated children, of three ethnic groups and all born to mothers with chronic alcoholism, had in common defects of the face and skull, limbs and heart, with growth deficiency beginning before birth and delayed development. The authors present this as apparently the first reported link between maternal alcoholism and abnormal formation of the child's body; the Introduction credits Ulleland (ref. 1, a co-author) with having already drawn attention to growth deficiency and developmental delay in such children. Journal issue dated 9 June 1973.

anchors.locator: Clinical Findings › Methods of Patient Ascertainment, 1st paragraph (left column, continues in the right column)
anchors.extracted: All eight were assembled and examined together by the same two authors (K.J. and D.W.S.). Four were recognised first as sharing a pattern; two more were found through the features seen in the first four; the last two were found because their mothers had chronic alcoholism. No comparison group; examiners knew the mothers' histories.

anchors.locator: Clinical Findings › Methods of Patient Ascertainment, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: All mothers met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism. Every mother drank heavily for the whole pregnancy (no quantities given); the mothers of patients 1 and 7 were in hospital with delirium tremens during it, and patient 3 was born while her mother was in an alcoholic stupor. None had a known addiction to another drug; smoking is not mentioned.

Duration of maternal alcoholism 7, 3, 4, 11, 2+, 10, 23 and 15 years (mean 9.4; recomputed 75/8 = 9.375); delirium tremens 5 of 6 with data (2 unknown); cirrhosis 2 of 6; nutritional anaemia 2 of 6; maternal age at birth 22 to 40 (mean 31.7; recomputed 31.75); weight change in pregnancy: loss of 1, 5, 15 and 5 lb in four mothers, gain of 19 and 30 lb in two, unknown in two; gestational age 34 to 44 weeks (mean 38; recomputed 38.4); birth weight 1,550 to 2,500 g (mean 2,034; recomputed 2,033.5); birth length 38 to 47 cm (mean 43.6; recomputed 43.55); breech 3 of 8; Apgar scores 4/4 to 9/10. Checked on the rendered page.

anchors.locator: Table II (header: patient number and ethnic group); case reports, pp. 1267–1268
anchors.extracted: Patients 1 to 3 Native American, 4 to 6 Black, 7 and 8 White. Case reports: patients 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7 are girls, 5, 6 and 8 boys (five girls, three boys).

anchors.locator: Table II (Pattern of anomalies, Total column); case reports
anchors.extracted: Present out of 8: developmental delay 8, microcephaly 7, prenatal growth deficiency 8, postnatal growth deficiency 8, short palpebral fissures 8, maxillary hypoplasia with relative prognathism 7, epicanthal folds 4, joint anomalies 5 (elbow, finger-joint and hip limitation or dislocation), altered palmar crease pattern 6, cardiac anomaly 5. Per-child marks and the case reports agree: cardiac anomalies were an atrial septal defect confirmed by catheterisation (patient 2), a patent ductus arteriosus (4) and systolic murmurs that disappeared, read as closed ventricular septal defects (1, 3, 8). Checked on the rendered page.

All had prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency. Mean gestational age 38 weeks, but mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks respectively. None caught up in growth, neither while in hospital for failure to thrive (six children, with adequate calorie intake documented) nor in foster care (three). After age 1, average growth in length 65% and weight gain 38% of normal (normal = 50th percentile of the Stuart charts, Fig. 4 legend; Fig. 4 shows seven children; the number behind the averages is not stated). Mean daily weight gain 9 g against 26.6 g in upper-middle-class Seattle children and 24.4 g in high-risk children of a city programme, the latter two from a personal communication (ref. 3).
Head circumference below the 3rd percentile for gestational age at birth in 7 of 8; by age 1, below the 3rd percentile for height age and for chronological age in 5 of the 6 with data.

anchors.locator: Table III (Mental, motor and social development) with footnotes; Performance, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 1269)
anchors.extracted: Age at testing 3 to 57 months (14, 3, 57, 46, 18, 40, 48, 34). IQ or mental development index 59, 83, 75, 57, 79 and 70, below 50 in patient 8; patient 5 assessed on the Denver scale only, with no index. Tests: Stanford-Binet for patients 3, 4, 6 and 7, Bayley for 1, 2, 4 and 8. Testing by one author (A.P.S.) for all but patient 5. By the authors' reading no child scored in the normal range, and social and motor levels tracked mental age more than actual age; fine motor problems in 5 of the 6 tested; repetitive self-stimulating behaviour in 5. Checked on the rendered page.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (continues in the right column)
anchors.extracted: The authors say earlier animal and human evidence had not clearly shown an association and that this report argues strongly for one; the similarity suggests one cause, probably some still unidentified consequence of the mothers' alcoholism (direct ethanol toxicity first, or a breakdown product or another agent in the drinks). Maternal undernutrition is considered and argued against: such severe prenatal growth deficiency with this set of malformations had not been described in children of undernourished mothers who did not have alcoholism.

Length was more affected than weight at birth, the reverse of the usual picture after general maternal undernutrition, which the authors take to suggest a cause other than nutrition alone; lack of catch-up despite adequate intake in hospital or foster care is taken to mean that the postnatal deficiency was not due to deprivation as such.

Microcephaly in 7 of 8 without catch-up; the authors find it hard to say how far the socioeconomic situation or continued maternal drinking affected development; all the families were on welfare, though parents' education ranged from 8th grade to college and occupation from unskilled to professional; patients 1 (foster care from birth) and 3 (foster care from age 2 to 4) did not perform better.

Variable severity is expected; two children have partly affected siblings born while their mothers had alcoholism, others have siblings said to be normal (born before or after the mothers' alcoholism began). The report describes the more severely affected children and deliberately leaves out possibly mild cases. The authors conclude their data are "sufficient to establish that maternal alcoholism can cause serious aberrant fetal development".

Supported by Maternal and Child Health Services (Health Services and Mental Health Administration, US Department of Health, Education and Welfare, project 913), NIH grant HD 05961 and the National Foundation–March of Dimes; no conflict statement. Information on patient 5 was supplied by Akron Children's Hospital (Ohio), and that child was examined personally by D.W.S.
The pattern is referred to only as a syndrome; the name fetal alcohol syndrome appears nowhere in the article (all five pages read; text layer searched).

key_findings.correction: Last sentence: no amount of drinking is given, and timing only in general terms (excessive drinking throughout the pregnancy, as the finding itself says), with no detail by stage of pregnancy or pattern. The same wording ('amounts and timing were not recorded') in cannot_establish should be adjusted in the same way.

reporting_issues.note: Re-found blind (acknowledgements, p. 1271; Performance, p. 1269; Table III footnote, p. 1270).
Checked on the rendered Table III footnote: patient 4 is listed under both the Stanford-Binet and the Bayley mental scale.
Checked: values 30, 36, 35 and 23 at testing ages 46, 40, 48 and 34 months, labelled in months.
Checked: case-report ages 4 y 3 mo, 2 y 6 mo and 3 y 9 mo against testing ages 57, 34 and 48 months; the other children differ by 1 to 2 months.
Checked: patient 8's murmur was noted until 1 year of age (p. 1268), while the Discussion places closure before 1 year (p. 1270).
Checked: Fig. 5 legend gives only the Nellhaus band for normal males; Fig. 4 is labelled patients 2 to 8.

risk_of_bias.note: Case series with no applicable instrument; the editors' domains and the overall high judgment are agreed (selection partly on the features, mild cases excluded, unblinded examiners who knew the mothers' histories, no comparison group, alternative explanations unmeasured).

interpretation_gap.note: Rating 'substantial' agreed. One correction to 'claimed': the Summary hedges the priority claim (the report seems to be the first reported association, p. 1267); the card's quotation drops the hedge and so states the authors' claim more firmly than they did. The closing causal sentence (p. 1271) is quoted correctly and is the real gap.

missed: The journal issue date, 9 June 1973 (p. 1267 header), is not on the card; the claim relies on it to contrast this report with the reviews' November 1973 date for the first description of FAS.

Maternal weight loss during pregnancy in four of the six mothers with data (Table I) is recorded under exposure but not in a key finding or in the risk-of-bias note on alternative explanations, although it bears directly on the undernutrition explanation the authors argue against.
